titleStmt.title: The dual-path code paradigm for time-deterministic and efficient networked embedded systems

analytic.title: The dual-path code paradigm for time-deterministic and efficient networked embedded systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The single-path code paradigm [1] has been conceived to generate real-time code that is highly temporally predicable, making worst-case execution time analysis trivial. The software/hardware architecture proposed in [2], which only supports a time-triggered message interface, builds on the singlepath code paradigm and static scheduling of tasks. The presented execution model in that paper yields software that is time-predictable by construction, and therefore supports timepredictable communication in a networked system.

In this paper, we present the dual-path code paradigm that extends the execution model presented in [2]. In particular, this paradigm improves schedulability of an end-system, through the notion of observable event [3], [4], and supports energy efficient scheduling of regularly polling tasks at these end-systems, by exploiting the 1-1 correspondence between (input) events and (output) responses of tasks. The dual-path code paradigm is therefore particularly suitable for the construction of timedeterministic and efficient networked hard real-time embedded systems.

div.head: A. Background and motivation
div.p: In [2], a software execution model based on the single-path code paradigm [1] and static scheduling of tasks is described, that can be used to build networked hard real-time subsystems that are time predictable. Such an approach is a cornerstone to build time-deterministic networks with scheduled end-systems and switches. As an example, the IEEE 802.1 standards that are under development by the Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) Task Group [5], support time-deterministic networks through Time-Aware Shapers (TAS) [6] and a network-wide time-synchronization protocol [7]. These extensions for realtime communication over Ethernet are aimed at the automotive and industrial automation domains, amongst others. How to schedule real-time communication in such networked systems is presented in, for example, [8]. Analysis for end-systems based on basic single-rate cyclic executives is addressed in, for example, [9], [10] for a basic real-time system model M B and [11], [12] for a refined model M R .
Part of this work has been performed in the context of the PENTA Call 3 project 17006 HiPer (High Performance Vehicle Computer and Communication System for Autonomous Driving).

div.head: B. Problem description
div.p: From the basic single-rate cyclic executives considered in [10], the single-rate periodic cyclic executive yields energy efficient scheduling of tasks with limited finalization jitter for the basic real-time system model M B . Compared to that basic model, the refined model M R presented in [11] yields improved schedulability of systems. The approach does not prevent (output) response jitter, however.

Although the single-path code paradigm [1] yields deterministic task execution, it gives rise to problems when combined with the models presented in [9], [11], amongst others. Firstly, the paradigm gives rise to optimistic best-case analysis for the basic model M B , as described in [11]. Secondly, the paradigm doesn't comply with the refined model M R . Thirdly, (output) responses of subsystems are not necessarily time-deterministic. Fourthly, and finally, the paradigm is not energy efficient, by always enforcing worst-case computation times of tasks.

The execution model presented in [2] resolves the first three problems, albeit potentially at the cost of an increase of the time at which these responses are provided. As a result, schedulability of systems is therefore potentially decreased compared to [1]. Moreover, the fourth problem (energy inefficiency) is not resolved, making the approach less applicable for networked embedded systems.

div.head: C. Contributions
div.p: This paper presents (i) the dual-path code paradigm, an extension of the single-path code paradigm, and (ii) the required extension of the execution model to support time-deterministic and efficient networked hard real-time embedded systems. We illustrate the schedulability and energy improvement of the dual-path code paradigm compared to the single-path-code paradigm [1], [2] based on the single-rate periodic cyclic executive and its analysis [10], [12]. Finally, we show that this novel paradigm requires a revision of the refined model M R and gives rise to a specialization with time-predictable computation times.

div.head: D. Organization
div.p: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The basic and refined real-time system models are recapitulated in Section II. Section III recapitulates the single-rate periodic cyclic executive and its schedulability analysis for both system models, and compares the models for a single-rate periodic cyclic executive from a scheduling perspective. The dualpath code paradigm is presented in Section IV. The refined model is revisited and revised in Section V. Implementation considerations are presented in Section VI. Further enhancements are discussed and a brief comparison with related approached is presented in Section VII. The paper is concluded in Section VIII.

div.head: II. RECAP OF REAL-TIME SYSTEM MODELS
div.p: In this section, the basic model M B presented in [9] and the refined model M R presented in [11] are recapitulated.

div.head: A. A basic real-time system model M B
div.p: We assume a system S, a set E S of n sporadic (input) events e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e n , a set R S of n (output) responses r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r n to these events, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Each event e i is characterized by a minimal interarrival time WT S i . Each event-response tuple e i , r i is characterized by a best-case system deadline BD S i and a worst-case system deadline WD S i , where 0 ≤ BD S i ≤ WD S i ≤ WT S i . Moreover, we assume a set T S of n independent, 'regularly' polling tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , where task τ i senses event e i and provides response r i . Each task τ i is characterized by a bestcase computation time BC i and a worst-case computation time WC i , where 0 < BC i ≤ WC i . The execution of a task is termed a job. A job of task τ i is denoted by ι i,k , with 0 ≤ k, i.e. the first job of τ i is denoted by ι i,0 . The computation time C i,k of every job ι i,k of task τ i shall be between BC i and WC i , i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∧ 0≤k BC i ≤ C i,k ≤ WC i .
div.p: We use s i,k and f i,k to denote the start time and the finalization time of job ι i,k , respectively. The start jitter SJ i of a task τ i is defined as the maximum deviation of the start-times of a task from a strictly periodic pattern, i.e.
div.formula: SJ i = sup 0≤k ∧ 0≤ ((s i,k -k × T i ) -(s i, -× T i )) ,
div.p: where T i denotes the (hypothetical) period of the task. The finalization jitter is defined similarly, i.e.
div.formula: FJ i = sup 0≤k ∧ 0≤ ((f i,k -k × T i ) -(f i, -× T i )) .
div.p: We assume that tasks are executed on a single processor, are scheduled by a basic cyclic executive, run non-preemptively and do not suspend themselves. The sequence of tasks executed in a cycle is assumed to be known statically. Moreover, we ignore scheduling overhead and system initialization.
For ease of presentation and without loss of generality, the jobs of tasks in a cycle are assumed to be executed in the order of increasing index, i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i<j≤n ∧ 0≤k s i,k < s j,k . B. A refined real-time system model M R
div.p: The basic real-time systems model can be refined by taking the notion of observable event [3], [4] 1 into account. The last observable event of a task (in our case a response) need not be at the end of a task's execution. Moreover, a job of a task does not necessarily provide a response, i.e. given the 1-1 correspondence between events and responses, there will be no response when a job does not detect an event.
To address these two aspects, the model can be refined by distinguishing additional notions of best-case and worst-case computation times of a task τ i , e.g.
• BC r i and WC r i : the best-case and worst-case computation time for task τ i to provide a response, respectively;
• BC nr i and WC nr i : the best-case and worst-case computation time when no response is given (i.e. no event is detected) by τ i . For these additional notions, we assume2
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i ≤ BC r i ≤ WC r i (1)
div.p: and
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n WC nr i ≤ WC i ,(2)
div.p: because providing a response may take time. Moreover, whenever no event is detected, there is probably not much that needs to be done, hence
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i = BC nr i ≤ WC nr i .(3)
div.p: Finally, because a task may still perform some work, like a state information update [3], [4] or clean-up operations [14], after providing the response, we have
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n WC r i ≤ WC i .(4)
div.p: Based on these three notions of computation time, we define three notions of computation jitter of a task τ i :

• CJ nr i : variations in computation times of jobs without response, i.e. CJ nr i = WC nr i -BC nr i ; • CJ r i : variations in computation times of jobs till the provision of a response, i.e. CJ r i = WC r i -BC r i ; • CJ i : variations in computation times of jobs till the finalization (or completion), i.e. CJ i = WC i -BC i . We use r i,k to denote the response time of job ι i,k , i.e. the time at which the job provides a response (if any). We introduce an overloaded predicate exists() that takes one or more response times r i,k of jobs ι i,k of task τ i and holds if and only if all its arguments exist, i.e. those jobs detected (input) events e i and produced (output) responses r i . We therefore have
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∧ 0≤k exists(r i,k ) ⇒ r i,k ≤ f i,k .
div.p: The response jitter is defined similar to the start jitter and finalization jitter, but requires a precondition that the response times exist, i.e.
div.formula: RJ i = sup 0≤k ∧ 0≤ ∧ exists(ri,k,ri, ) ((r i,k -k × T i ) -(r i, -× T i )) .

div.head: III. SINGLE-RATE PERIODIC CYCLIC EXECUTIVES AND THEIR ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, we briefly recapitulate single-rate periodic cyclic executives [10] and its schedulability analysis for both the basic model M B [10] and the refined model M R [12]. We conclude the section with a brief comparison of the models for the single-rate periodic cyclic executive from a scheduling perspective.

div.head: A. Recap of single-rate periodic cyclic executives
div.p: We assume that every task is started at the worst-case starttime relative to the start of the cycle, assuming each task needs its worst-case computation time. The sum of the worst-case computation times of all tasks shall be less than the cycle time T S , otherwise the (worst-case) executions of the tasks do not 'fit' in a cycle, i.e.
div.formula: 1≤i≤n WC i ≤ T S .
div.p: Figure 1 illustrates a single-rate periodic cyclic executive with cycle time T S , where the cycle is started at time Φ. Under a single-rate periodic cyclic executive, the start time s i,k of job ι i,k is exactly defined by
div.formula: s i,k = s 1,0 + k × T S + 1≤j<i WC j = s i,0 + k × T S .
div.p: Stated differently, every task is started strictly periodically, i.e. ∀ 1≤i≤n SJ i = 0, making scheduling highly deterministic. A task τ i may experience limited finalization jitter FJ i , however, due to its computation jitter CJ i , i.e.
div.formula: FJ i = CJ i . (5

div.p: We make the following three observations when comparing the schedulability conditions for M R and for M B . Firstly, the best-case schedulability condition (8) for M R is independent of a specific cyclic executive, like the best-case schedulability condition in (7) for M B . Secondly, M R allows more systems to meet the best-case schedulability condition than M B , because of (1). Thirdly, the worst-case schedulability condition (9) for M R considers an extended worst-case situation, whereas the worst-case schedulability condition in (7) for M B only considers the initial situation. As a result, the worst-case schedulability condition (9) for M R looks considerably more complicated than the condition for M B . We take a closer look at the worst-case analysis of both models in the next subsection.

Despite the fact that ( 9) for the refined model M R is considerably more complicated than the right conjunct of (7) for the basic model M B , the only difference between (11) and (10) is the superscript 'r' in the term WC r i in (11).

div.head: D. A comparison of models
div.p: Theorem 3. (Theorem 7 in [12] without proof) From a scheduling perspective, the refined model M R dominates the basic model M B for the single-rate periodic cyclic executive.

Proof. The result follows immediately from the observations that (i) M R can schedule more systems to meet the best-case schedulability condition than M B , because of (1) and that (ii) (11) of Theorem 2 for M R implies (10) of Theorem 1 for M B , because of (4).

From this theorem, we conclude that (i) the 1-1 correspondence between (input) events and (output) responses can be exploited to improve the best-case schedulability of a system, and (ii) the notion of observable event [3], [4] may improve the worst-case schedulability of a system S.

div.head: IV. FROM SINGLE-PATH TO DUAL-PATH CODE PARADIGM
div.p: In this section, we start with the single-path code paradigm presented in [1], and gradually extend that approach towards the dual-code paradigm by incorporating the notion of observable event and exploiting the 1-1 correspondence between (input) event and (output) responses.

div.head: A. Preventing response jitter
div.p: Without additional means, a task τ i will typically experience computation jitter CJ r i for responses and computation jitter CJ i for finalization, which gives rise to response jitter RJ i and finalization jitter FJ i under a strictly periodic cyclic executive; see ( 6) and ( 5), respectively. The single-path code paradigm [1] prevents computation jitter CJ i for finalization, by guaranteeing ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i = WC i . Moreover, the paradigm also prevents computation jitter CJ nr i when no response is given, i.e. ∀ 1≤i≤n BC nr i = WC nr i . The computation time till finalization is even the same with or without a response, i.e. ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i = BC nr i = WC nr i = WC i It is not guaranteed, however, that a task τ i does not experience computation jitter CJ r i for responses, because different paths may exist in the code that provide a response, i.e. it may happen for a task τ i that BC r i < WC r i , hampering time-deterministic transmission of messages in a networked hard real-time embedded system. Moreover, it may happen for a task τ i that BC r i < BC i . This has two consequences. Firstly, it means that assumption (1) of the refined model doesn't hold. Secondly, the best-case schedulability condition of the basic model M B may yield an optimistic result for a system S, i.e. may deem a system schedulable whereas it is not [11].

The execution model described in [2] in addition prevents computation jitter CJ r for responses, by having the actual data transfer for output under control of the operating system, and scheduled after the task execution. As a result,
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i = BC nr i = BC r i = WC nr i = WC r i = WC i .
div.p: This not only prevents response jitter of tasks, but also resolves the problems with (1) and the best-case schedulability condition for M B .

div.head: B. Improving worst-case schedulability
div.p: In its basic form, the execution model described in [2] does not support the notion of observable event [3], [4]. We propose to support the notion by 1) using the predictable task preemption supported by the execution model and 2) extending the operating system support.

Let every job of a task be defined as a sequence of two subjobs, a first sub-job yielding a response (if any), and a second sub-job performing finalization actions (if any). Moreover, let a data transfer for output also be supported by the operating system after a sub-job execution. Through such additional support we may get ∀ 1≤i≤n BC r i = WC r i ≤ BC i = WC i , still preventing response and finalization jitter of tasks, whilst facilitating observable events. Through this extension of the operating system, the worst-case schedulability of systems can be improved. Unfortunately, assumption (1) of the refined model M R again doesn't hold and the best-case schedulability condition of the basic model M B may again yield an optimistic result for a system S.

By splitting each job in a sequence of (non-preemptive) subjobs, the task model is similar to the model described in, for example, [13] for cooperative scheduling and [15] for fixedpriority scheduling with deferred preemption.

div.head: C. Improving energy efficiency and best-case schedulability
div.p: A disadvantage of the single-path code paradigm as described in [1], [2] is that the execution of each job will always require its worst-case computation time. Moreover, experience reveals that the worst-case computation time required for the 'single-path' code is typically larger than for 'regular' code [16]. To mitigate these disadvantages, we may exploit the notion of modes of tasks, as described in [16]. By distinguishing two modes for a task, i.e.
1) a no response mode whenever a task does not detect an event and therefore doesn't produce a response, and 2) a response mode whenever a task detects an event, we get
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i = BC nr i = WC nr i and ∀ 1≤i≤n BC r i = WC r i ≤ WC i .
div.p: Unfortunately, assumption (1) of the refined model M R need not hold, because it is not guaranteed that ∀ 1≤i≤n BC nr i ≤ BC r i .
Introducing modes has three advantages. Firstly, we may gain back on energy efficiency; see the next lemma.
Lemma 1. Whenever a system S is schedulable under a single-rate periodic cyclic executive for the refined model M R with a cycle time of T S , a fraction f S,gain (T S ) given by
div.formula: T S - 1≤i≤n WC i T S ≤ f S,gain (T S ) ≤ T S - 1≤i≤n BC i

div.head: T S of the time can be used for background processing by a singlerate periodic cyclic executive (or to save energy by temporally reducing the clock speed).
div.p: Proof. The term T S -1≤i≤n WC i represents the worstcase (i.e. minimum) amount of spare time 4 in a cycle and the term T S -1≤i≤n BC i represents the best-case (i.e. maximum) amount of spare time. The result therefore follows immediately.

For the single-path code paradigm as described in approach [1], [2], ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i = WC i , hence the fraction f S,gain (T S ) is exclusively based on the slack time, because the gain time is zero. With the introduction of modes, the upper bound on the fraction may increase substantially.
Secondly, the 1-1 correspondence of (input) events and (output) responses can be exploited to improve the best-case schedulability of a system.

Thirdly and lastly, there is no need to split every job into two sub-jobs. Whereas a preemption is required to have an output generated by the operating system in the response mode after the completion of the first sub-job, there is no need for a preemption for the no response mode.

div.head: D. The dual-path code paradigm
div.p: The dual-path code paradigm essentially combines the three steps described above: 1) it prevents response jitter by building on the single-path code paradigm [1] and its execution model [2]; 2) it improves worst-case schedulability by supporting the notion of observable event [3], [4] through a) predictable task preemption [2] and b) extended operating system support for (output) responses after sub-job completion; 3) it improves best-case schedulability and energy efficiency by exploiting the 1-1 correspondence between (input) events and (output) responses through the introduction of dedicated modes for tasks [16] for executions with and without responses.
This novel paradigm (and its support) results in a timedeterministic and energy efficient system. Unfortunately, this paradigm doesn't comply with the refined model M R .
V. REFINED MODEL M R REVISITED AND REVISED

In the previous section, we identified that the single-path code paradigm and the dual-path code paradigm do not comply with the refined model M R , in particular assumption (1) need not hold. In this section, we revisit the refined model and propose a (simple) revision, yielding a revised model M R .
For the revised model M R we propose to lift the assumption ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i ≤ BC r i , i.e. to change (1) into
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n BC r i ≤ WC r i .
div.p: Without proof, we claim that both the best-case and the worst-case schedulability analysis of a system do not change compared to the analysis for the refined model M R , because neither analysis depends on the lifted assumption. It does mean, however, that a theorem similar to Theorem 3 doesn't exist for the basic model M B and the revised model M R . The dual-path code paradigm gives rise to a specialization of the revised model M R by having time-deterministic computation times for 1) jobs without responses, i.e. ∀ 1≤i≤n BC nr i = WC nr i , 2) responses of jobs, i.e. ∀ 1≤i≤n BC r i = WC r i , and 3) jobs with responses (being WC i for each such job).

Note that for the dual-path code paradigm, tasks have timedeterministic computation times per mode. As a result, 1) the response jitter of each task is zero, which is required for time-deterministic communication, i.e. ∀ 1≤i≤n RJ i = 0, but 2) neither the finalization jitter nor the computation jitter need to be zero, i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n FJ i = WC i -BC i ≥ 0 and ∀ 1≤i≤n CJ i = WC i -BC i ≥ 0.

div.head: VI. IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS
div.p: Single-or dual-path code generation is part of a customized code compilation process that aims at generating timepredictable real-time code. For the real-time programmer who uses a single-or dual-path compiler, coding is no different from coding in any other SW development environment that hosts a real-time compiler and WCET analysis -the source code needs to be WCET-analyzable and is exactly the same.

In the following, we describe the concept of single-path code and its extension to dual-path code and dual-path code generation in more detail. We will show that the use of singlepath or dual-path code does not imply a limitation on task coding or semantics and we will demonstrate that the move from single-path to dual-path is straight-forward using existing code generation and analysis techniques.

div.head: A. Generating single-path code
div.p: Single-path code generation compiles program code in such a way that the generated executables do not have any control-flow decisions that depend on the code inputs, i.e., the compiler determines the invariable flow of control during code compilation. At runtime, the generated code follows the same trace of instructions (=single path) for all possible inputs that may be provided. When single-path code is executed on a processor that provides an invariable timing for all instructions (again, regardless of the operands of the instructions), all snippets of single-path code and therefore entire tasks are executed with constant execution times. These constant execution times, which are necessarily also the task WCETs, are repeatable [17] and can be obtained by a simple WCET analysis or even in a single execution-time measurement [1].

Single-path code does not use conditional control-flow instructions to implement input-data specific changes of the program state during a computation. Instead, it uses predicated instructions to enable or disable individual instructions conditionally. While the processor executes the same sequence of instructions every time a task executes, the semantics of the individual instructions is controlled by the states of their predicates, which reflect the truth values of the conditions of the code. In single-path code, the predicated instructions take over the role that conditional control-flow branches together with conditionally executed blocks of instructions have in regular machine code. Thus, any semantics that can be implemented in traditional code by means of input-dependent control-flow branches can also be realized in single-path code.
The single-path code generation mainly builds on the code transformation patterns called if conversion, loop conversion, and function conversion.

If conversion translates code that would traditionally have branching semantics and thus variable execution time into sequential code that uses predicates and executes in constant time (see Figure 2).

Loop conversion eliminates the timing variability of loops by making them iterate a constant number of times. Loops that would otherwise iterate a variable number of times are compiled such that they always use up the maximum number of i f ! cond goto L e l s e x = v a l 1 ( cond ) x = v a l 1 goto Lend ( ! cond ) x = v a l 2 L e l s e : . x = v a l 2 . Lend : . . . . . iterations. To keep the original semantics, however, predicates disable the loop body once the required number of iterations has been reached. The third pattern, function conversion, replaces function calls with calls to new functions where a new predicate parameter has been added to the original parameter list. The new functions are predicated versions of the original functions, and the predicate parameter is used to pass the predicate from the call context into the function body. This facilitates the predicated execution of the function. For a detailed description of the single-path code generation strategy, see [18].

div.head: B. Task implementation and predictable preemption
div.p: Figure 3 shows a source-code task template for our model M R . Depending on whether an input event e i has been detected or not, task τ i has two sub-jobs or just one. When τ i detects an input event, i.e., input detected(e i ) = true, which corresponds to mode 1 (the response mode), τ i executes two sub-jobs that are separated by the preemption point() system call. In the first sub-job, produce response() realizes the computation of the response r i and writes it to its output buffer. Later, when the preemption point system call has terminated and the sub-job has completed the operating system reads the output buffer and provides the response to the environment. The second sub-job performs the respective finalization of τ i in finalize 1(). When τ i does not detect an input event it executes in mode 2 (the no response mode). In this case, it only consists of one sub-job that finalizes the task in finalize 2(). The system call preemption point() implements time-predictable task preemption. In mode 1, the call separates the two sub-jobs of τ i by returning control to the operating system. This realizes a fixed preemption point [2] that adds τ i to the OS queue of preempted tasks, thus finishing the first sub-job after a fixed time and returning control back to the cyclic executive. The cyclic executive executes the second sub-job of τ i by issuing the respective resume call as planned before runtime.

div.head: C. Modes and dual-path code generation
div.p: As mentioned before, tasks execute in one of two modes and behave differently depending on whether an input has been detected or not. The task implementation reflects these modes by testing this condition in the input detected() system call, i.e., the preconditions for the execution of the two modes of a task are input detected(e i ) = true and input detected(e i ) = false, respectively.

To improve best-case schedulability and energy efficiency, dual-path code generation provides two different, modespecific traces (= execution paths) to implement the divergent semantics and sub-job structure for each of the modes. To this end, dual-path code generation uses the same strategy as for single-path code, except that the mode condition, input detected() is translated into a conditional branch and not converted into predicated code; so this is the only inputdependent (= mode dependent) branch in the task code.

To exploit the different mode timings for the task timing analysis and the creation of schedules, a mode based WCET analysis (see [19], [20]) evaluates the two mode-specific paths and computes the execution times of the sub-jobs of both modes. Alternatively, the execution times of the sub-jobs could be assessed by executing the dual-path code for each mode (i.e., running it once when executing with an input e i and again without an input) and measuring the respective execution times of the sub-jobs.

div.head: VII. DISCUSSION
div.p: In this section, we describe further enhancements and briefly compare our approach with related approaches.

div.head: A. Further enhancements
div.p: In this paper, we focussed on so-called 'strict' single-rate periodic cyclic executives, where each task is activated by a timer, and a real-time system model where (input) events and (output) responses have a 1-1 relationship. Whenever the model is enhanced by also considering classical control tasks that read a (continuous) value from a sensor and always write a (continuous) value to an actuator, it makes no sense to distinguish the two modes described for the dual-path code paradigm for these tasks. These control tasks therefore always execute for their worst-case computation times. As a result, the next task in the sequence can simply be started after such a control task completes, without requiring a dedicated timer expiration. This provides options to reduce the implementation overhead by using 'non-strict' single-rate periodic cyclic executives [10]. Further investigation falls outside the scope of this paper, however.

div.head: B. A comparison with related approaches
div.p: Based on [3], [4], [21]- [24], amongst others, it is described in [25] how the worst-case schedulability (or latency) of classical control tasks can be improved and their (sampling and) response jitter can be reduced. Similar to our approach, all communication in [24], [25] is done by the kernel, i.e. timetriggered, resolving the problem of jitter. Unlike our approach, these existing approaches assume online scheduling, i.e. fixed priority scheduling (FPS) and/or dynamic priority scheduling (using EDF), instead of off-line (i.e. static) scheduling based on a cyclic executive.

The approach in, e.g. [25], still faces a problem when a task does not complete before its deadline, however, e.g. due to the fact that the assumed worst-case computation time is optimistic, i.e. too small, [26]. Overrun handling is therefore considered a topic of future work in [25]. This limitation has been resolved in our work.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, (i) the dual-path code paradigm, an extension of the single path code paradigm [1], and (ii) the required extensions of the execution model [2] have been presented, to support time-deterministic and efficient networked hard realtime embedded systems. Schedulability improvements were gained through (i) the support of predictable task preemption, allowing a job to be split in a sequence of sub-jobs, (ii) the support of (output) responses of sub-jobs by extending the operating system, and (iii) the support of modes of tasks. The support for modes of tasks also enabled energyefficiency improvements. The dual-code paradigm requires the refined model M R to be revisited and revised, however. Fortunately, the revision turned out to be simple. For the resulting revised model M R the existing analysis for the refined model M R [11], [12] can be reused. The schedulability and energy-efficiency improvements of this novel paradigm have been illustrated through the single-rate periodic cyclic executive and its analysis. We are inclined to believe that this novel paradigm is particularly useful for systems based on time-deterministic networks, such as IEEE 802.1 TSN enabled switches in an Ethernet network with TAS [6] and network-wide time-synchronization [7], combined with static scheduling of tasks at end-systems.
As future work, we aim at further refinements of the real-time system model and options to further reduce the implementation overhead of an end-system.
